section_1.title: The Intuition: Points vs. Perspectives
section_1.content: Establish prerequisite: A coordinate system is just a grid. Explain that a point in space is absolute, but its numerical 'address' depends on the axes (basis) we choose. Use an animation of a character (a robot) moving across a grid.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot standing on a square grid. If we rotate the floor, the robot hasn't moved, but its 'x' and 'y' coordinates relative to the new walls have changed.

section_2.title: Defining the Basis Matrix
section_2.content: Introduce the Change of Basis Matrix (P). Explain that if basis B = {v1, v2}, any vector can be written as a linear combination: v = c1v1 + c2v2. Visually represent this as a 'Translation Dictionary' that maps coordinates from the B-basis to the Standard basis.
section_2.example: If Basis B is made of two vectors at 45 degrees, the matrix P uses those vectors as columns. P converts 'coordinates in B' into 'standard coordinates'.

section_3.title: The Transformation Mechanics
section_3.content: Focus on the formula [v]_std = P[v]_B. Use a flow animation: a vector in space, a coordinate system grid shifting, and the matrix multiplication acting as the bridge between the two numerical representations.
section_3.example: A GPS coordinate system vs. a local park coordinate system. The same landmark (the vector) has different numbers, linked by the matrix P.

section_4.title: Inverting the Perspective
section_4.content: Address the inverse process: How to find coordinates in basis B if we have the standard ones. Introduce P^-1. Emphasize that switching basis is reversible as long as the basis vectors are linearly independent.
section_4.example: A camera zooming out: If you know how the world looks from the camera's tilted angle (B), you can use P^-1 to calculate how the world looks from the 'upright' standard view.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Summary
section_5.content: Summarize the 'Change of Basis' as a simple change in perspective. Reinforce that the vector remains invariant (it doesn't change length or direction), only our description of it changes.
section_5.example: Final visual: A cat sitting in the center of the room. Two observers stand at different corners, recording the cat's position using different rulers. The cat is the 'vector', the observers' setups are the 'bases'.
